steps.observation: Write a short story about a lighthouse keeper.

steps.action:
Keeper of the Third Point Light

Every night, when the horizon dissolved into ink, Elias Thorn unlocked the iron door of Third Point Lighthouse and stepped onto the spiral stair. He counted forty-seven echoes of his boots before reaching the lantern room—a ritual as old as the wrinkles in his oil-skin coat.

Outside, the sea was restless. Waves shouldered one another, eager to be first against the black basalt cliff. Elias trimmed the lamp’s wick, polished the Fresnel lens, and sparked the mantle alive. A cone of gold swept the dark, stitching a path for ships he would never see.

Loneliness, some said, was a lighthouse keeper’s only true companion. But Elias disagreed. He had wind for conversation, gulls for gossip, and the faithful heartbeat of the lamp for company. While others spoke in words, he spoke in flashes—three longs, one short—Third Point’s signature. Somewhere out there, captains read his Morse of light and felt the night loosen its grip.

One stormy December evening, as thunder rolled like boulders across the sky, the lamp faltered. Salt spray had crept into the gears, and the lens trembled. Elias wrestled with the mechanism, but the wind fought him, slamming the glass panes like angry shutters.

Suddenly, between gusts, he spied a lone fishing trawler, lights extinguished by rain, tilting dangerously near the reef. Desperation gripped him. If the lamp went dark now, the reef would claim them.

He fetched the brass hand-crank—an antique seldom used—and locked it into place. Every rotation felt like wringing water from stones, but the lens obeyed, turning at his pace. Flash. Darkness. Flash. Darkness. His shoulders burned, yet he kept the cadence. Minutes blurred into aching hours.

At dawn, the storm retreated, and a slow pink hush spread across the sea. Exhausted, Elias slumped against the wall. Through the glass, he saw the trawler anchored safely in the cove, crew waving hats toward the lighthouse. They never knew the name of the man whose muscles were their metronome in the night; they knew only the light.

Elias allowed himself one small smile. He counted forty-seven steps down to his kitchen, brewed strong coffee, and watched the sun climb the sky. Another night conquered, another silence kept. And far offshore, in logbooks crusted with salt, captains would mark that Third Point Light burned steady through the storm, never realizing it was not machinery, but a man, who proved constant when the world went dark.
